:::note[Written against main]
This page follows `main` at 9d25dc1, and it differs from the copy in HotLoop 4.17.0, the latest release. Parts of it may be newer than what you have installed. The [release notes](/releases/) say what moved.

Added in 4.11.0. `internal/broker` lets this Gateway run its own MQTT broker
in-process, so a small, single-box HotLoop install has nothing extra to
deploy. Off by default (`HOTLOOP_BROKER_ENABLED`): a deployment that already
runs Mosquitto or EMQX has nothing to point this at, and starting a second
broker beside one that already exists is not a safe default to guess into
existence.

## Why this exists

`internal/edgepublish` (this Gateway acting as a Sparkplug edge node) and
`internal/fleet` (tracking registered edge relays) both connect *outward* to
an MQTT broker over `BrokerAddress`, they have never run one themselves.
That is fine when a deployment already has a broker, whether that's an
existing Mosquitto instance or one run alongside HotLoop for other reasons.
It is not fine as the *only* option: this project exists to cut the
number of moving parts a plant floor depends on, and requiring a second piece of
infrastructure just to get a Sparkplug hub running for one Gateway would be
adding a moving part back in through the side door.

With `HOTLOOP_BROKER_ENABLED=true`, this same process listens for MQTT
connections on its own address. `internal/edgepublish`, `internal/fleet`, or
an external edge relay's `HOTLOOP_EDGE_PUBLISH_BROKER` can all be pointed at
`localhost:1883` (in-cluster, the Gateway's own Service address) instead.

## When to use this, and when not to

**Use it** for a single Gateway, a handful of edge relays, and traffic
volumes an embedded broker sharing a process with the historian, the
alarm engine and the HTTP API can comfortably absorb, the common case this
whole project targets: one plant, one box, minimal infrastructure.

**Do not use it** as a substitute for a production-grade broker at real
scale: multiple independent Sparkplug host applications, very high fan-out,
bridging between sites, or workloads that need clustering, horizontal
scaling, or a broker's own dedicated operational tooling (detailed metrics,
dynamic ACLs, plugin ecosystems) are all real reasons to run Mosquitto,
EMQX, or another dedicated broker instead, and to point this Gateway's own
`EdgePublishConfig`/`FleetConfig` at it like any other deployment already
can. This package does not compete with that use case; it exists for the
deployments that would otherwise have no broker at all.

## Logins, and what each one may touch

Three kinds of login get in, and they are not equal.

**Logins made in HotLoop** (Settings, MQTT, or `/api/broker/logins` in
[API.md](/iot/api/)) carry rules: the topics the login may publish to and the
topics it may subscribe to. `%u` in a rule is the login's own name and `%p` the
discovery prefix. They start from a profile and are yours to edit after:

| Profile | Publish | Subscribe | For |
|---|---|---|---|
| `shelly` | `%u/#`, `shellies/announce` | `%u/#`, `shellies/command`, `%p/status` | a Shelly Gen2 or later, login named after its MQTT topic prefix |
| `esphome` | `%u/#`, `%p/+/%u/+/config`, `esphome/discover/%u` | `%u/#`, `%p/status`, `esphome/discover` | an ESPHome node, login named after the node |
| `tasmota` | `tele/%u/#`, `stat/%u/#`, `tasmota/discovery/+/config`, `tasmota/discovery/+/sensors` | `cmnd/%u/#`, `cmnd/tasmotas/#` | a Tasmota device, login named after its topic |
| `zigbee2mqtt` | `%u/#`, `%p/#` | `%u/#`, `%p/status` | a Zigbee2MQTT bridge, login named after its base topic |
| `integration` | nothing | `#` | a dashboard, a historian, you with MQTT Explorer |
| `full` | `#` | `#` | anything, the whole plant |

Name a Shelly's login after its topic prefix and it can announce itself and
report as itself, and that's it. It can't publish to `cmnd/boiler/POWER`, it
can't announce a device in somebody else's name, and it can't subscribe to `#`
and read the plant. The broker checks every publish, every subscription, and
every message on its way out to a subscriber, so a rule can't be stretched with
a clever wildcard. A last will is checked too, when the client connects: the
broker library publishes wills without asking anyone, so a login whose will
points somewhere it may not publish doesn't get in. Otherwise a cheap plug
could leave a retained `ON` on the boiler and pull its own power cord.

A change to a login holds from that client's next packet. Narrow a login and
its connected device loses the topics right then; delete one and the client
still hanging on can do nothing at all, and can't connect again. Passwords are
bcrypt hashes in `broker_logins`, which is in every backup; the API never
answers with either.

Zigbee2MQTT is the odd one: one bridge announces every device on its radio, so
its profile may publish anywhere under the prefix. That's the bridge's job, and
it's why the Discovered screen shows who announced what.

**`HOTLOOP_BROKER_USERS`** is the old list of `user:password` pairs (only the
first colon splits, so a password may contain one). These can do anything, on
every topic, exactly like 4.16 and 4.17. That's on purpose: nobody upgrades
into a plant whose Sparkplug traffic suddenly bounces off an ACL they never
wrote. It also means each of those logins is a key to the whole plant. Move
devices to logins made in HotLoop and keep the env ones for the things that
really need everything: the fleet, an edge relay, the edge publisher. Checked in
constant time; a username with the wrong password is refused.

**Anonymous** (`HOTLOOP_BROKER_ALLOW_ANONYMOUS`, default `false`) is anything,
for anyone who can reach the port. It's a per-deployment opt-in for a trusted
LAN or a test rig, never something this process decides is fine on its own,
and the Discovered screen says so in red while it's on. It doesn't loosen
anything for a client that does send a username: a wrong password is still a
wrong password.

A broker with no `HOTLOOP_BROKER_USERS` and anonymous off starts fine. Until
somebody makes a login in HotLoop, the only thing that can connect is HotLoop.

Other brokers are their own business. On Mosquitto or EMQX, the ACLs are that
broker's to enforce, the same boundary [FLEET.md](/gateway/fleet/) draws, and
[DISCOVERY.md](/iot/mqtt-discovery/) has an ACL for HotLoop's own login there.

## Discovery, and HotLoop's own login

With the broker on, HotLoop listens on it for devices that announce
themselves (see [DISCOVERY.md](/iot/mqtt-discovery/)). The broker notes which login and
client published each discovery config. The Discovered screen shows it, and a
device accepted from one login that gets announced by another is held for a
person, with a warning in the log ("Kitchen re-announced by login garage-node;
it was accepted from kitchen-node"). Either somebody moved the device to a new
login, or a login is pretending to be a device it isn't. A person decides
which.

HotLoop's own client on this broker (the discovery listener, and the drivers of
discovered devices) logs in with a login the broker makes at every start and
keeps only in memory. It can do anything. There is nothing to configure for
it, nothing on disk, and nothing in a backup; it is a different one after every
restart.

## TLS

A plain TCP listener (`HOTLOOP_BROKER_LISTEN_ADDR`, default `:1883`) is
always available once the broker is enabled. Setting
`HOTLOOP_BROKER_TLS_ENABLED=true` with `HOTLOOP_BROKER_TLS_CERT_FILE` and
`HOTLOOP_BROKER_TLS_KEY_FILE` adds a second, independent listener
(`HOTLOOP_BROKER_TLS_LISTEN_ADDR`, default `:8883`) terminated with that
certificate. Both listeners run at once when TLS is enabled, nothing closes
the plaintext one, so an operator who wants TLS-only reachability enforces
that at the network layer (a NetworkPolicy, a firewall rule), the same way
this chart already leaves broader network exposure decisions to
`networkPolicy.ingress` rather than the application deciding on its own
which of its own ports may be reached.

This mirrors the reasoning `internal/notify.SMTPChannel`'s STARTTLS fix
documents for the alarm-notification SMTP channel: a broker that only ever
accepts credentials in plaintext is not a smaller version of that problem, it is the same one, and arguably more direct, since here this process is the
side of the connection actually asking for a password. Unlike the SMTP
channel's in-band STARTTLS upgrade of a single connection, the broker's TLS
listener is a second, separate socket, the same shape Mosquitto, EMQX and
most MQTT brokers use for a plaintext port alongside a TLS one, and the more
natural fit for MQTT, which (unlike SMTP) has no widely-implemented in-band
upgrade of its own.

This package does not generate a certificate of its own, self-signed or
otherwise, nothing downstream would end up trusting one it invented, so a
real certificate (from an internal CA, `cert-manager`, or any other source)
is always the operator's to provide.

## Configuration

| Variable | Default | <span class="sr-only">Details</span> |
|---|---|---|
| `HOTLOOP_BROKER_ENABLED` | `false` | The feature is off until this is set |
| `HOTLOOP_BROKER_LISTEN_ADDR` | `:1883` | The plaintext TCP listener |
| `HOTLOOP_BROKER_TLS_ENABLED` | `false` | Adds a second, independent TLS listener |
| `HOTLOOP_BROKER_TLS_LISTEN_ADDR` | `:8883` | Only used when TLS is enabled |
| `HOTLOOP_BROKER_TLS_CERT_FILE` / `_KEY_FILE` | n/a | Required when TLS is enabled |
| `HOTLOOP_BROKER_ALLOW_ANONYMOUS` | `false` | Per-deployment opt-in; never set this by default |
| `HOTLOOP_BROKER_USERS` | none | `user:password,user2:password2`. Each can do anything; see above. Logins with rules are made in HotLoop |
| `HOTLOOP_BROKER_DISCOVERY` | `true` | Listen for devices announcing themselves; see [DISCOVERY.md](/iot/mqtt-discovery/) |
| `HOTLOOP_BROKER_DISCOVERY_PREFIX` | `homeassistant` | The topic prefix announcements arrive under |

## Startup ordering

`cmd/hotloop/main.go` starts the broker immediately after the polling
runtime, before the Sparkplug edge publisher and the fleet manager. Both of
those already retry their own broker connection on failure, so this ordering
is not required for correctness, but an operator pointing either of them at
this same process's own address has no reason to lean on that retry when
starting the broker first costs nothing and removes the race entirely.

## What has and has not been verified

**Tested**, not **verified**, see this repository's own distinction between
the two. The broker is tested with a real
[`eclipse/paho.mqtt.golang`](https://github.com/eclipse/paho.mqtt.golang)
client, the same client `internal/edgepublish` and `internal/fleet` already
depend on, driving an embedded broker instance started for each test on an
OS-assigned loopback port:

- A correctly-credentialed client connects, publishes, and a second
  correctly-credentialed, subscribed client receives the message.
- A registered username with the **wrong password** is refused.
- An **unregistered username** is refused.
- An **anonymous** connection is refused when `AllowAnonymous` is `false`,
  and accepted when it is `true`, and a registered username with a wrong
  password is still refused even when `AllowAnonymous` is `true`, proving
  anonymous access does not loosen credential checking for a client that
  does present credentials.
- Every profile held to its topics: what it may publish arrives, and a
  command topic, another device's topics, a config in another device's name,
  Sparkplug and `#` don't. A login hears only what its rules cover. A last
  will outside its rules keeps it out. A narrowed or deleted login loses the
  topics on the next packet. `HOTLOOP_BROKER_USERS` logins and HotLoop's own
  still publish and subscribe to Sparkplug, the fleet's topics and `#`.
- Who published each config: recorded for configs that got through, not for
  refused ones or state topics, and never more than 4096 topics.
- A real TLS client, configured to trust a generated test certificate,
  connects successfully over the TLS listener.
- A **plaintext** connection to the TLS listener's port fails cleanly
  (the TLS handshake never completes) rather than being silently accepted
  or left hanging.

Manually run end to end against the compiled `hotloop` binary with
`HOTLOOP_BROKER_ENABLED=true`, connecting a real client over the network to
publish and subscribe across the plaintext listener, not just through
`go test`.

**Not verified** against any MQTT client other than the paho Go client, not,
for example, `mosquitto_pub`/`mosquitto_sub`, a certified Sparkplug host
application, a different language's MQTT client library, or MQTT 5-only
client behavior. `mochi-mqtt/server/v2` itself claims to pass the Paho
interoperability test suite for both MQTT v3 and v5; this repository has not
independently re-run that suite. Also not verified: behavior under the kind
of sustained high-throughput or high-fan-out load a dedicated broker is built
for, see "When to use this, and when not to" above.
